question: A 3-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presents to the clinic with a 4-day history of acute onset cough. Her parents have recently started to introduce several new foods into her diet. Her vital signs are all within normal limits. Physical exam is significant for decreased breath sounds on the right. What is the most appropriate definitive management in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "possible respiratory obstruction" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "consider foreign body aspiration" -> "definitive management requires visualization of airway" -> "rigid bronchoscopy is appropriate" -> 85%

CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "recent introduction of new foods" -> "possible allergic reaction or aspiration" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "indicates potential obstruction" -> "need for airway evaluation" -> "rigid bronchoscopy is the best option" -> 80%

CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "vital signs normal" -> "physical exam shows decreased breath sounds" -> "suggests localized issue in the lungs" -> "could be due to foreign body" -> "requires direct visualization" -> "rigid bronchoscopy is definitive" -> 90%

CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "acute onset suggests sudden event" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "indicates possible foreign body" -> "need to confirm diagnosis" -> "rigid bronchoscopy allows for removal" -> 88%
analysis: The acute onset cough in a 3-year-old girl, along with decreased breath sounds on the right, raises suspicion for a foreign body aspiration or possibly a pneumonia. Given the recent introduction of new foods, the likelihood of aspiration is increased. Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive management for suspected foreign body aspiration in children, as it allows for direct visualization and removal of the foreign object. Other options like CXR or bronchodilators may be useful but do not provide definitive management.
